title: We grew a Malayalam page from zero with a system built in Claude.
line: A brand-new faceless Instagram page, in a niche language, run day to day by AI we trained.
statCap: Instagram followers in 20 days, from zero
client: Stories in Earth, [@stories.in.earth](https://www.instagram.com/stories.in.earth/) on Instagram (our own page)
role: Co-founder, strategist and system builder, with Agrajh AK
where: Built in New York, for a Malayalam audience
channels: Instagram Reels only, made vertical so they could also go to TikTok and YouTube Shorts
brief: Brands want more content on more platforms with the same team. My co-founder Agrajh AK and I wanted to know how far a small, AI-run system could take a page that started with nothing.
So we set it a hard test: a brand-new page with no history and no followers, in Malayalam, the language of Kerala. A niche audience, and a hard language to get right.
idea: Run a faceless page like a format, not a feed: one repeatable shape that every reel follows, made by a system that does the daily work.
The shape has three beats: something every Malayali has at home, one fact they never knew about it, and a twist at the end so they stay to the last second.
how: Built the whole pipeline in [Claude](https://claude.ai/) and [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code), with a skill we trained for each job: finding topics that already work in the niche, writing the script, animating it and writing the caption.
Animated every reel as a 3D scene in code: objects, rooms, light and Malayalam type, with no people on screen.
Narrated every reel in Agrajh's voice, cloned with [ElevenLabs voice cloning](https://elevenlabs.io/voice-cloning), so the page sounds like one person.
Let the system write the caption, with the hook up front, and handle the posting. Instagram [labels the reels as AI content](https://help.instagram.com/761121959519495), and we keep it that way.
result: 5,842 followers on November 24, 2026, twenty days after the first reel. About 5,000 of them came in the first week.
2,095,734 views and 1,522,275 viewers in the last 30 days, with 99.3% of the views from people who didn't follow the page.
The fourth reel, [Cyanide in kappa?](https://www.instagram.com/reel/Dfbq2ckSnge/), passed 1.6 million views and about 57,000 likes.
218,322 interactions from 103,866 accounts in 30 days.

p: Agrajh AK and I co-founded Growvior together, and the page didn't start as a case study. It began as a playful way to promote one of our own AI products, a tool that turns a script into a narrated stickman video. Within days the audience made it something else: people followed for the stories, not the product, so we let the page become its own thing. Agrajh gave his voice once to build the clone with ElevenLabs. Every reel since is narrated by that clone, and he hasn't recorded a single reel himself.

The first reel went up on November 4, 2026, asking what would happen to Kerala if the Western Ghats vanished overnight. Three days later the fourth reel, [Cyanide in kappa?](https://www.instagram.com/reel/Dfbq2ckSnge/), took off: 1.6 million views, about 57,000 likes and 260 comments. Most of the page's followers arrived in the week around it.
The full breakdown, with all twelve reels and what each one did, is in [the write-up](/work/how-we-grew-a-malayalam-page-from-zero/).

99.3% of the views came from people who didn't follow the page. That's how Reels is built: Instagram's head, Adam Mosseri, explains in [Instagram Ranking Explained](https://about.instagram.com/blog/announcements/instagram-ranking-explained) that each part of the app runs its own ranking, and that Reels, like Explore, mostly shows people accounts they don't already follow.

So a brand-new page isn't starting from zero reach. It's starting from zero trust. Every reel has to earn a stranger's attention in the first second and keep it to the last, which is exactly what the three-beat format is for.
Every reel is a small lesson about something Malayalis already know. These are the facts behind them, with sources, so anyone can check the work.
ul: **Cyanide in kappa?** Raw cassava carries cyanogenic glycosides, mainly linamarin, that release cyanide when the root is cut. Peeling, soaking and cooking bring it down to safe levels, which is why the way Kerala cooks kappa matters ([FAO](https://www.fao.org/3/t0207e/T0207E08.htm)).

**The code on your gold.** Since July 1, 2021, every hallmarked gold piece in India carries a six-digit HUID, the Hallmark Unique Identification, and it can be checked in the BIS Care app ([Bureau of Indian Standards](https://www.bis.gov.in/hallmarking-overview/hallmarking-faqs/hallmarking-faq)).
**Kochi was born in a flood.** A great flood of the Periyar in 1341 silted up the old port of Muziris and opened the natural harbour at Kochi ([Kochi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kochi)).
**Water in a coconut.** Coconut water is the fruit's liquid endosperm, which slowly turns into the white flesh as the nut matures ([Coconut water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_water)).
**A needle inside chembu?** The itch from raw taro comes from microscopic needle-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate called [raphides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphide).

**A paddy field below the sea.** Kuttanad farms rice 1.2 to 3 metres below sea level, and the FAO has listed it as a [Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System](https://www.fao.org/giahs/giahs-around-the-world/india-kuttanad-farming-system/en) since 2013.

**Kanyakumari to Assam on one train.** The [Dibrugarh-Kanyakumari Vivek Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dibrugarh%E2%80%93Kanyakumari_Vivek_Express) crosses India from its southern tip to Assam.
**What if the Western Ghats vanished?** The range is a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1342) and shapes Kerala's monsoon, rivers and forests.
**Kollam's black sand.** The beaches around [Chavara in Kollam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chavara) hold mineral sands rich in ilmenite, rutile, zircon and monazite.
**Cashews in the shell.** The [cashew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cashew) shell holds a caustic oil that can burn skin, so nuts are roasted and shelled before they reach a shop.

**Sabarimala aravana.** The prasadam keeps because it's made with very little moisture; in 2026, tins dried too far to stretch shelf life [turned hard](https://www.onmanorama.com/news/kerala/2026/01/08/sabarimala-aravana-production-jaggery-issue.html).

after.h: What any brand can take from this
ul: **Follow the audience, not the plan.** The page was meant to promote a product. When people showed up for the stories instead, we let the stories lead.
**Pick a format before a feed.** Three beats every time: something people own, one fact they never knew, a twist at the end.
**Start at home.** On this page, food and things in the house beat places on a map.
**Find the hidden danger.** A risk inside something safe made the biggest hook.
**Write for strangers.** 99.3% of the views came from people who didn't follow the page, so every reel has to work for someone seeing it first.
**Keep the AI label on.** People stay for the story, not the trick.
**Plan the second hit.** One reel can make a page's first week. The work after that is finding the next one.

**Take it beyond one page.** We only run it on Instagram, but every reel is vertical, so the same system could post to TikTok and YouTube Shorts too, in other languages, for FMCG, food brands and chains, tech products and real estate. We're building it now for [Levin Reji](https://www.instagram.com/realtorlevin/).

after.h: The same system, built for a client
p: The first client build is for [Levin Reji](https://www.instagram.com/realtorlevin/), a real estate agent with eXp Realty in Pennsylvania. GTA 6 launched on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and the whole internet was talking about Vice City, the game's version of Miami. Two days later, Levin's page posted a reel asking what a house costs in the real Vice City.

It answers with real numbers. The typical single-family house in Miami-Dade sold for $706,000 in October ([Miami Realtors, via Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/miami-home-sales-plunge-but-rebound-could-be-on-the-way-12732781)), and the typical Philadelphia home sold for about $279,000 from July to September ([Redfin](https://www.redfin.com/city/15502/PA/Philadelphia/housing-market)), so one Miami house costs more than two Philly homes. The twist is for his own audience: Philadelphia homeowners get a real-life cheat code, the [Homestead Exemption](https://www.phila.gov/services/property-lots-housing/get-the-homestead-exemption/), worth up to $1,399 a year off their Real Estate Tax, with a December 1 deadline.

It follows this page's explainer format and runs on the same toolkit. Claude drafted the script, checked every number and built the animation, and the voice is Levin's own, cloned in ElevenLabs from recordings he sent. His compliance rules travel with every reel: eXp Realty's name and phone at the same size as his, his Pennsylvania license line, and a note that the reel isn't affiliated with Rockstar Games.
It's the hype piece in the hub, hype and hygiene plan I pitched Levin in February, and his page is early. By November 26 the reel had passed 1,600 views on an account with 549 followers.

ul: **What is Stories in Earth?** A faceless Malayalam explainer page on Instagram, [@stories.in.earth](https://www.instagram.com/stories.in.earth/), started on November 4, 2026 by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil and [Agrajh AK](https://www.linkedin.com/in/agrajh-ak/), the co-founders of [Growvior](https://growvior.com/).
**How fast did it grow?** From zero to 5,842 followers in 20 days, with 2,095,734 views in its last 30 days and one reel at 1.6 million views.

**Is it made with AI?** Yes. Scripts, 3D animation, captions and posting run on a system built in Claude, and the narration is Agrajh's voice cloned with ElevenLabs. People chose the niche, the format and the rules, and Instagram's AI label stays on.

**Can a brand get the same system?** Yes. title: A possession in a packed cinema.
line: A horror trailer is easy to ignore. A possession in the seat next to you isn't.
statCap: news outlets covered it in three days
client: Sony Pictures Entertainment India, through WLDD
role: Creative Strategist, founding team at WLDD
where: Bangalore, for a release across India
when: April 2023, the week The Pope's Exorcist opened in India
channels: A live stunt in a cinema, short-form video, earned press
brief: Sony Pictures India was opening [The Pope's Exorcist](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt13375076/), Julius Avery's horror film with Russell Crowe as the Vatican's chief exorcist, Father Gabriele Amorth, in Indian cinemas on April 7, 2023, [in English, Hindi, Tamil and Telugu](https://www.outlookindia.com/art-entertainment/-the-pope-s-exorcist-trailer-unravels-vatical-conspiracy-through-a-young-boy-s-possession-news-264794). Horror trailers all promise the same thing, and audiences have learned to scroll past the promise.

I had pitched and closed Sony Pictures as WLDD's first international client, so the first release had to prove that a fifteen-person agency in Bangalore could make a Hollywood film the thing people talked about.
idea: Don't tell people the film is scary. Let them watch a room full of people get scared.
We staged a possession in a packed cinema while the trailer played, so the reaction itself became the ad.
how: Built the stunt around the trailer: a woman in a white gown, apparently possessed, crawling through a real audience at a real screening while the trailer played.
Filmed the room's reaction as it happened, so the scare on screen was real.
Released the clip so it travelled as something that had happened in a cinema, not as an ad, and let people pass it on.
result: The clip went viral across India in the week the film opened.

[News18](https://www.news18.com/buzz/the-popes-exorcist-trailer-brings-horror-to-life-as-possessed-woman-jumps-out-in-theatre-7496905.html), [India Today](https://www.indiatoday.in/trending-news/story/woman-acts-possessed-while-trailer-of-the-popes-exorcist-plays-in-movie-theatre-video-is-viral-2357066-2023-04-07), [Hindustan Times](https://www.hindustantimes.com/trending/woman-scares-people-in-theatre-as-the-pope-s-exorcist-trailer-plays-on-screen-101680956103411.html), [The Indian Express](https://indianexpress.com/article/trending/trending-in-india/possessed-woman-growls-at-moviegoers-as-the-popes-exorcist-trailer-plays-in-theatre-8545834/), [SheThePeople](https://www.shethepeople.tv/viral-video/woman-acts-possessed-the-popes-exorcist) and [LatestLY](https://www.latestly.com/socially/social-viral/the-popes-exorcist-trailer-combined-with-possessed-woman-turns-theatre-into-horror-hall-watch-video-5047593.html) all covered it between April 7 and April 9.
Sony stayed. The relationship grew to cover 65, Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse and Insidious: The Red Door.
lesson: People share a reaction faster than they share an ad. Design the reaction.
proof: My article on why it worked
Peekwire interview: the stunt, in Nivedkrishna's words

story.h: Why a fifteen-person agency could pull it off
p: WLDD was fifteen people on one floor in Bangalore when this happened. We had big clients, bigger ambitions and very little to protect, which meant an idea that made people in a larger agency nervous could actually get made, and fast.

The idea came from knowing how Indian audiences watch horror: loudly and together, and half the fun is watching the person next to you jump. So we didn't advertise the film. We staged the experience of watching it, in a room full of strangers, and let the reaction be the ad.
I wrote the full story of what it taught me, five lessons on virality, in [What the Pope's Exorcist taught me about virality](/work/what-the-popes-exorcist-taught-me-about-virality/).

after.h: What any film marketer can steal from this
ul: **Market the moment, not the movie.** People don't share a trailer. They share what happened to someone while it played.
**Make it feel like news, not an ad.** The headlines led with a woman scaring a cinema, and every one of them carried the film's name.
**Local beats global.** It worked because it was built for how this audience watches horror, not for audiences everywhere.
**If the idea doesn't make someone nervous, it won't travel.** Safe ideas get approved and forgotten.
**Shorten the approval path.** The moment has a half-life measured in hours, so the people closest to the culture need room to move.

title: We gave Durex a fan page instead of an ad.
line: A premium brand page that couldn't make memes, and a fan page that could.
client: Durex India, through WLDD in Bangalore
brief: Durex India's own Instagram is a premium brand page. Memes, skits and trend jokes are the content that travels fastest on Indian Instagram, but they didn't belong on the main page.
We wanted that reach, with the kind of humour Duolingo uses on its own page, without touching Durex India's feed.
idea: Build Durex a separate IP: Thank You Durex, a page that calls itself Durex's fan page and asks [@durex.india](https://www.instagram.com/durex.india/) to notice it.
A fan can joke in ways a brand can't. Every skit, trend and meme puts the product in the frame, and the joke does the selling.
how: Used memes as hooks, then built skits, trends and collabs around them.
Durex sent us their products, and we wrote the jokes around them.
Ran collabs with our own ad parody page, which remade ads as jokes, to bring more polished content into the mix.
Put the team in front of the camera when a skit needed it. I'm the last person in the 20.9 million view reel.
result: One reel, posted on May 20, 2023, passed 20.9 million views, with 453,000 likes and 2,410 comments.
Two more pinned reels from that spring passed [6.2 million](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CsB2XhpAD9P/) and [5.8 million](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CrBfiSBAddN/) views.
The page is still running, with 149,000 followers in November 2026.
lesson: When the brand page has to stay premium, give the jokes a home of their own.

story.h: Why a brand needed a fan
p: [@durex.india](https://www.instagram.com/durex.india/) is a premium brand page, and it has to stay one. But the content that travels fastest on Indian Instagram is memes, skits and trend jokes, the kind a premium page can't post without losing what makes it premium.

So we gave the jokes a home of their own. Thank You Durex calls itself Durex's fan page and asks @durex.india to notice it. A fan can say things a brand can't, and every skit still puts the product in the frame. The humour sits closer to the way Duolingo runs its own accounts than to a brand campaign: self-aware, a little unhinged and made to be sent to a friend.

Durex sent us products, and we wrote the jokes around them. When a skit needed a face, the team stepped in front of the camera, which is how I ended up as the last person in the 20.9 million view reel.

after.h: What any premium brand can steal from this
ul: **Split the voice, not the brand.** Keep the main page premium and give the humour its own page, with its own name and its own rules.
**Write the fan's point of view.** A page that wants the brand to notice it can tease, beg and joke in ways the brand itself can't.
**Use memes as the hook, not the whole post.** The meme stops the scroll; the skit, trend or collab around it is what people send on.
**Collaborate with pages that already have the audience.** Our ad parody page remade ads as jokes and brought a more polished edge into the mix.
**Keep the product in frame.** The joke does the selling only if the product is in the joke.

title: I ran the agency's page like a client's.
line: An agency that made brands go viral, with a page that didn't show it.
statCap: the views on a typical reel
role: Creative Strategist, founding team at WLDD
brief: WLDD sold meme marketing to Netflix India, Prime Video, Zomato and Swiggy. Its own Instagram, [@wldd.in](https://www.instagram.com/wldd.in/), had about 2,000 followers, and a typical reel got about 4,000 views.
Clients, creators and the people we wanted to hire all looked at that page before they talked to us. It had to look like the agency it was selling.
idea: Run the agency's page the way we ran a client's: [hub, hype and hygiene](/work/hub-hype-and-hygiene/), with the office as the cast.

Hub was the everyday: office skits, memes about agency life and trends we could shoot in an afternoon. Hype was the big moments: festivals, awards, events. Hygiene was the plain information: who we are, what we do and who we're hiring.
how: Posted about 100 reels in sixteen months, around one every five days.

Put the team in front of the camera: [WLDD wali Holi](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CpkfY7FMJpe/), an [office cricket match](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CqidrvJPfA_/), an [AI Avengers takeover](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CuHcPUXMnof/) and [different versions of life at WLDD](https://www.instagram.com/reel/C5WB0L2pH2A/).

Turned agency news into content: a [best movie and web series promotion award](https://www.instagram.com/reel/Cs81FZouXH4/), a [Prime Video event with AP Dhillon](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CwDIv7fBUA4/), a [hiring fest in the office](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CyV-JoDys38/) and [our first creators fest](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CzJVdvESERE/).
Wrote every caption the way we wrote for clients: short, quirky and made to be sent to a friend.
result: A typical reel went from about 4,000 views in 2022 to about 19,000 in early 2024, almost five times the reach.
In 2022, 8 of 82 reels passed 10,000 views. In my sixteen months, 56 of 100 did. From January to April 2024, every single one did.

The biggest were [a visit from Shraddha Kapoor](https://www.instagram.com/reel/C2ud1KUSkEZ/) at 85,000 views, [Life at WLDD](https://www.instagram.com/reel/C5WB0L2pH2A/) at 76,000 and [WLDD wali Holi](https://www.instagram.com/reel/CpkfY7FMJpe/) at 58,000.
Followers went from about 2,000 to about 11,000. The page has 28,600 today.

story.h: The agency, from fifteen people to a media group
p: WLDD, short for Wubba Lubba Dub Dub, was founded in 2018 by three college friends from Belgaum, Arihant Jain, Jaidev Kesti and Vivekanand Kilari, and [raised $1.2 million from Negen Capital](https://inc42.com/buzz/wldd-acquires-creative-studio-imagined) in 2023. I joined as one of the first fifteen people in its Bangalore office, all on the top floor of one building.

I watched it take the second floor, then the first, then the whole building, then a second building for its creator marketing school. In February 2025 it [bought ScoopWhoop](https://www.storyboard18.com/brand-makers/meme-marketing-agency-wldd-buys-scoopwhoop-from-the-good-glamm-group-in-all-cash-deal-57487.htm) from The Good Glamm Group, and it has since bought the sneaker brand 7-10 and the creative studio Imagined. I wrote about those early days in [I joined WLDD when it was fifteen people on one floor](/work/fifteen-people-on-one-floor/).
An agency growing that fast needs its own page to keep up: every client, creator and hire checks it before they call.

after.h: What any agency can steal from this
ul: **Treat your own page as client one.** Brief it, plan it and report on it the way you would for a paying brand.
**Cast the office.** Your team is free, always available and more believable than any actor in a skit about agency life.
**Turn agency news into content.** An award, a client event or a hiring drive is a reel, not a press release.
**Post on a rhythm.** About one reel every five days for sixteen months gave the audience, and the algorithm, something to expect.
**Split the mix.** Roughly half [hub, about a third hype and the rest hygiene](/work/hub-hype-and-hygiene/) kept the page fun without losing who we are and who we're hiring.

title: Every video got a job.
line: An AI memory app with a founder who could talk, and Shorts nobody was watching.
client: Fetchy, an AI memory assistant you text over iMessage or SMS, from Marina del Rey, Los Angeles
role: Creative Strategist and Content Lead: strategy, scripts, direction, edit and posting
brief: [Fetchy](https://heyfetchy.com) saves your notes, links, tasks and ideas into a personal vault when you text it, and finds them again when you ask. Its co-founder and CEO, Nina Duong, found me on Handshake in December 2025, while the app was still in private release.
Her [YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@fetchyapp/shorts) had two or three Shorts, averaging 600 to 1,000 views each. The product was good; the videos weren't giving anyone a reason to stop.
idea: Stop posting at random. Give every video a job.

A hub, hype and hygiene plan: some videos build trust, some build community, and some chase the trends and audio breaking that week. And put the founder on camera, because a person explaining why they built something is more watchable than a feature list.
how: Nina asked for a small paid test first. I sent back a full content strategy she hadn't asked for: static post ideas, short-form scripts, a scripted street-interview series and a plan for posting across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube.
Built the [hub, hype and hygiene](/work/hub-hype-and-hygiene/) plan across all three, reusing every short-form asset on each platform instead of making each one from scratch.
Wrote the scripts and directed Nina's phone shoots shot by shot: head angles, where to place the camera, when to cut, and which high-performing reels to frame each shot against.
Edited every video from her raw footage, picked the trending audio, wrote the captions and tags, and posted, testing new placements on Instagram and YouTube as they rolled out.
Managed a video editor and a graphic designer on the account.
result: Shorts settled above 2,000 views each, against a starting average of 600 to 1,000.
One Short, [Happens all the time](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/FPO4kPOiFoY), passed 616,000 views.

Others followed: [When your boss says "food order"](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/QlvOMDUc954) at 12,000, [When you ask the universe for guidance](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/pq-02QHGgD8) at 11,000 and [I am not calm](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/KK7Z3mtLgoc) at 4,500.
The channel grew to more than 200 subscribers.
lesson: A content plan is a list of jobs. A video without a job is just a post.
quote: The results were real and, frankly, beyond what I expected from a brand-new hire.

story.h: Directing a founder from three time zones away
p: Nina is in Los Angeles. I'm in New York. So the shoots happened on her phone, and the direction had to be specific enough to work without me in the room.

For the best-performing videos, I didn't just write what she'd say. I wrote how to shoot it: which way to turn her head, where to put the phone, when to cut, and which reel to copy the framing from. She'd film it and send me the raw clips, and I'd build the video from there: the edit, the audio that was breaking that week, the caption, the tags.

The videos that travelled weren't feature demos. They were office comedy and relatable chaos, with Fetchy as the punchline: the boss asking for a food order, the morning that isn't happening, the person who chit-chats through every meeting. The product shows up as the answer, not the subject.
q: He wrote not only what I would say on camera but exactly how to shoot it.

after.h: What a founder-led brand can steal from this
ul: **Give every video a job before you shoot it.** Trust, community or reach. If you can't say which, don't post it.
**Direct the phone shoot like a film shoot.** A shot list with angles, cut points and a reference reel gets a founder's phone footage most of the way there.
**Lead with the situation, not the feature.** People share the joke about their boss. The app rides along as the punchline.
**Ride the audio while it's breaking.** Trending sounds lose their pull within days, so the edit has to turn around fast.
**Make once, post three times.** The same Short, captioned for each platform, went to YouTube, Instagram and TikTok.

title: A World Cup played on Avenue B.
line: A peri-peri restaurant, a city full of fans and a cup you could only get with dinner.
statCap: World Cup cups gone, each with an order over $35
client: Frangos Peri-Peri, two halal peri-peri restaurants in New York: Avenue B in the East Village and Hillside Avenue in Queens Village
role: Creative and Digital Marketing Strategist: strategy, shoots, design direction, copy, posting and paid ads
when: May to August 2026, through the FIFA World Cup
channels: Paid Meta (Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp), Instagram, TikTok, NYC Tourism + Conventions' World Cup dining program
brief: Rosina Ishaq started [Frangos](https://www.instagram.com/frangosnyc/) in 2015. She grew up in Britain, where peri-peri chicken is on every high street, and runs both restaurants herself: [182 Avenue B](https://evgrieve.com/2019/10/fowl-play-outpost-for-portuguese.html), open since October 2019 and [reviewed by The Infatuation](https://theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/frangos), and 233-16 Hillside Avenue in Queens.

The World Cup came to New York in 2026 and every restaurant with a screen wanted the same fans. Frangos needed a reason for them to pick peri-peri, and before any of that, it needed food footage good enough to sell with. That was Rosina's one condition: the food comes first.
idea: Make the restaurant part of the tournament instead of a place to watch it: an offer that only exists when a team wins, and a collectible that only exists with an order.
Then keep Frangos in whatever New York is talking about that week, while it's still fresh.
how: Started a WhatsApp group the night we agreed to work together, so every reference sat in one place, then filled it with nearly forty examples of food marketing to set the look.

Filmed more than a dozen dishes on my own Sony, stills and video, vertical and landscape, mostly in Queens on the quiet days early in the week: the whole chicken, quarters and thighs on the grill, wings, the chicken bites bowl, the [butter wrap](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dbe00eEMqXi/), shrimp skewers, [lamb chops](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dbb45Ugyt45/), the [kebab](https://www.instagram.com/p/DcKNGmRyHM_/) and the [Sunset](https://www.instagram.com/p/DbZOK1FSqhV/), smash and [chopped cheese](https://www.instagram.com/p/DavqD04yfSt/) burgers. One July shoot gave Rosina thirty-odd photos the same afternoon.
Directed editors and a designer in India, and turned every note around fast: when Rosina felt a burger edit looked too yellow, it was regraded and back within a day.
Took over Instagram on June 20 and restarted a TikTok that had sat untouched for two years, with 18 posts.

Wrote every caption to sell: the dish by name, both addresses, delivery range, a link to order direct instead of through the apps, then a block of the phrases people actually search, like "best smash burger in NYC" and "halal burger Manhattan".

Frangos' Queens restaurant was in [NYC Tourism + Conventions' Five Borough Winners Special](https://www.nyctourism.com/five-borough-winners-special/), the city's official World Cup dining program. When Portugal beat Uzbekistan 5-0, I built a match-day offer on the score: five wings and a free lemonade, under the line "Like it. Claim it."
Turned the city's collector cup into a paid Meta campaign geotargeted around Avenue B: a free World Cup cup with any order over $35.

Kept Frangos in the news cycle: a poster of the Empire State Building spire climbers holding a tray of chicken under "Bro... just order in," and [Wing Roulette](https://www.instagram.com/p/DbEYKSlyfOS/), a platter of mixed-heat wings turned into a dare to tag three friends.
result: All 50 cups went, so at least $1,750 in orders came in on the back of the campaign.
About 26 people claimed the 5-0 offer.
More than 30 reels and designed posts went out across Instagram and TikTok between late June and mid-August, most of them full dish films.
Frangos came out of the summer with a library of its own food footage and photos: reels, menu photos and the picture on its shop door.
lesson: Tie the offer to the moment. A deal that only exists because a team just won feels like news, not a discount.
quote: I am particular about how our food looks, and he never once argued with a note.

story.h: How a free cup became a campaign
p: Rosina got my number from Faisal and Sameer, who own Hyderabad Peri Peri in Brooklyn, and messaged me on May 15, 2026. I sent her my work that evening. We sat down on May 21 at the Avenue B restaurant, and afterwards I sent her designed posts I'd made for other cafés from my own food photos. Her first question was whether they'd been made with AI. They hadn't: I'd shot every one, and my editor had only fixed the light and added a backdrop.

The World Cup part happened fast. On June 24 our chicken bites bowl went up as game-day fuel. The next afternoon, the restaurant's limited-edition borough cups arrived: 24-ounce collector cups with a design for each borough, given only to places in the city's program, which [ran from June 11 to July 19](https://www.business.nyctourism.com/press-media/press-releases/five-borough-winners-special) with nearly 900 restaurants, bars and food spots. Rosina asked me for one picture of the free cup. I came back that evening with a match-day offer instead, built on Portugal's 5-0 win. She added a time limit and the rule that you had to like the post to claim it.

By the next morning the cup artwork was ready: a free World Cup cup with every order over $35. Then it became a paid campaign in Meta Ads Manager, aimed at the streets around Avenue B, so one ad reached people on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp instead of a post boosted from Instagram alone. Meta's verification for a small restaurant took us until nearly midnight. The ad was running the next day, and the cup offer carried on through July.

In early July, the couple who climbed the Empire State Building's spire were all anyone in the city talked about. I brought Rosina a poster of the climbers at the top with a tray of our chicken: "Bro... just order in." When she asked for last changes, my designer in India got up before sunrise to make them, and it was up that evening. Four days later we posted the quarter chicken with her own line: "More sauce than the World Cup."
q: Few people take direction that well and still bring the bigger ideas themselves.

after.h: What any restaurant can steal from this
ul: **Get the footage before the campaign.** A library of your own dishes, shot well, is what every offer, ad and post runs on. Without it, a good idea has nothing to wear.
**Build the offer on the score.** Five goals, five wings. An offer that only exists because something just happened reads as news, not a discount.
**Make the collectible the call to action.** People were already chasing the city's borough cups. Tying one to a $35 order gave them a reason to order more, not just to visit.
**Run paid through Meta, not the boost button.** One Ads Manager campaign reaches Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp at once, and lets you target the blocks around the restaurant.
**Write captions for the search bar.** The dish name, both addresses and the exact phrases people type, like "halal burger Manhattan", turn a post into something people find later.
**Answer the city's conversation the same day.** The spire poster worked because it went up while everyone was still talking about it.
